title: Impermanence
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley's main teaching is that everything in life is constantly changing and impermanent, including our thoughts, emotions, and experiences. This understanding can help us let go of attachment to things that are fleeting and unchanging, such as possessions or relationships, and instead cultivate a sense of acceptance and calm in the face of loss or change. By practicing mindfulness and meditation, we can develop a greater awareness of impermanence and respond to life's challenges with clarity and openness. This allows us to live more authentically and fully present in the moment, rather than being controlled by our attachments and expectations.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody, and welcome.
It's nice to see you all.
You were willing to venture out on a dark December night, and thank you, Kate and Jeff, for being here.
It's good to see you, too, on Zoom.
And if you can't hear me, let me know.
I'll try to speak up if I need to.
Tonight I'm going to talk mostly about impermanence, but I'm going to start out with a little bit about the three marks of existence, since impermanence is one of them.
The topic of the three marks, according to the Pali Canon, which was the first written record of the Buddhist teachings, was the second discourse that he gave.
And he said that all phenomena, including thoughts, emotions, and experiences, are marked by three characteristics.
Impermanence, the Pali word is anicca; suffering or dissatisfaction, dukkha; and not self, anata.
Understanding and appreciating the three marks of existence is a really important part of our practice.
So, impermanence: all things arise and cease.
That's their nature.
They come into being and they pass away.
The definition of anicca is seeing the arising and passing away of phenomena.
The second mark, dukkha, is usually translated as suffering, but also as dissatisfaction or unreliability.
And I prefer those two, actually.
When the Buddha said life is dukkha, he didn't mean that all of life is suffering.
And we all know that, because there's plenty of things in life that are wonderful, beautiful, and enjoyable.
What he meant is that the joys and beauty of life, a nice vacation, love, the natural world, a new car, a loved family member, and pets, don't last because they are also impermanent.
The vacation ends, the new car loses its shine, the close relationship can become strained or distant, the loved one dies.
So to depend on them and to cling to them for your happiness only leads to pain.
Nothing is permanent, including our lives.

The third mark, not self, and that is the translation of anata, is the hardest to understand and to experience in our day-to-day life, since every existence depends on things that are outside of itself for existence.
We need oxygen, we need sun and rain and dirt to grow food, trees need carbon dioxide.
There's no such thing as a separate, independent existence.
There's no such thing as an independent, unchanging self.
What we call a self is a bunch of physical, mental, and sensory processes that are interdependent and constantly moving and changing.

But because this third mark is so hard to understand and to see in life, the recommendation is to work mostly with the first two, with impermanence and dissatisfaction, and that can eventually lead to a better understanding of not self.
So now I'll switch over to just talking about impermanence.

In an article on that topic, Norman Fischer, who as most of you know is the founding teacher of Red Cedar Zen, but also the former abbot of the San Francisco Zen Center and the founder of Everyday Zen, said about impermanence:
*As far as classical Buddhism is concerned, impermanence is the number one inescapable and essentially painful fact of life.
It's the singular existential problem that the whole edifice of Buddhist practice is meant to address.
To understand impermanence at the deepest possible level, and of course we all understand it at a superficial level, and to merge with it fully is the whole of the Buddhist path.*

In the same article he quoted Eihei Dogen, the 13th century Japanese priest and considered founder of our style of Zen, Soto Zen, and Dogen said, *impermanence itself is Buddha nature.* And this means that impermanence isn't a problem to be overcome on the path, it actually is the path.
And practice isn't a way to overcome impermanence, it's a way to fully appreciate it and live it.
Another teacher, Gil Fronsdale, who teaches in the insight meditation tradition but started out as a Zen teacher, said that Buddhism is one big contemplation about impermanence.
And of course other religions and other traditions also talk about impermanence.
The Greek philosopher Heraclitus said that you can't step in the same river twice and there's nothing permanent except change.
In almost all of the reading and listening to Dharma talks that I did to prepare for this talk, there was an emphasis on practicing with impermanence.
That means noticing it in your day-to-day life and then noticing your reaction to it.

In our daily life there's weather, there are moods, there's night and day, there's all the changes in nature, plants growing and dying, the lawn needs mowing again, traffic jams, just an endless number of changes if you stop and just take a look around.
And that makes me wonder, do you ever just stop and be quiet for a little bit and look at all the changes that you might notice around you?
A bird flies by, or somebody drives by and the radio's playing a song, and it comes and goes.
I like to look at the sky a couple times a day because in this part of the world there are usually clouds and it's just beautiful to watch them slowly move across the sky.
One of the best places to pay attention to impermanence is in our daily meditation practice.
How each inhalation and exhalation starts and ends, how the body feels over time.
Your nose itches, but if you can leave it alone and just watch it, it'll eventually stop itching or something else will grab your attention.
And of course there's the endless flow of thoughts and feelings and memories and emotions that we can notice happening over and over again if we don't get caught up in one of them.
In one of his talks, Gil Frontsdale said that we are living in a world that is very different from the world that our mind constructs.

When we add our ideas, our stories, our projections and our desires and past experiences to the people and the things that we encounter, he said we create, he used this term, we recreate a virtual reality that is very different than what is actually right here right now.
Fixed ideas become a filter through which we see life.
I like, you don't need an electronic device to enjoy virtual reality, but that term really made me think a little bit about how I do that.
And I thought of a time a couple years ago at our eight-day meditation retreat on Samish Island.
I didn't sleep very well for probably five or six of those nights, and I don't like being tired at a session.
It's my least favorite thing, to start out in the morning really sleepy.
So the first morning I woke up and I'm like, oh god, I didn't sleep at all.
I'm really tired.
This is going to be a hard day.
This is going to be a long day.
I can't wait until the bell rings at 9 p.m. and I can come back here and try to get some sleep.
And of course when you want the day to go quickly, it goes really slowly.
And so that day was just exactly as I painted it.
It was a long, slow, uncomfortable day, and I was pretty unhappy.
Then the next night, I didn't sleep very well either, so I woke up again.
I was like, oh jeez, another tough day on the way here.
So we got to the Zendo and fortunately I was able to just drop my storyline about what kind of day I was going to have and just notice what day am I really having.
And it was surprising.
I was tired, sleepy, and then I had a period of time where I was quite alert.
I was like, oh, I'm alert.
And then I got sleepy again, and then I got alert again, and it was very different than I thought it would be.
And then later in the day, I was able to drop my unhappiness about being sleepy and my resistance to it.
I don't like this, that kind of thing, and just be okay with it.
Okay, I'm going to be sleepy today.
And that really made a difference.
I just had a day of some sleepiness, some alertness, some sleepiness, some alertness.
It's fine.
It was quite transformative.
And I could really see how I had painted myself a certain kind of day, and if I held on to that, that's the kind of day I was going to have.
So it was quite a useful exercise to see that.
I don't like long airplane rides.
And when we have a trip planned, I have to remind myself ahead of time: do not create this story of discomfort and inconvenience.
Just get on the plane and see what happens.
And almost always, the flights are much less uncomfortable than I think they're going to be.
So the mind often holds on to things long after those things have happened.
You might have a difficult encounter or an unpleasant conversation with someone and then go over and over and over it again, which makes it a whole lot longer.
And clinging to those kinds of things not only creates more suffering, but it also makes the world seem more solid than it is.
The world moves a lot more if we let go of some of our holding on to things.
Imagine if you have an argument with someone and, when the argument's over, maybe you look at it and think, what happened here?
Can I learn something from this?
And then you let it go, so that the next time you see this person, you're really open to whatever could happen.
As opposed to going over and over the argument, this is a certain kind of person, and then the next time you see them, oh God, here we go again.
So which kind of response would create less suffering for you and for other people?
A regular meditation practice can be very helpful in recognizing impermanence and finding out how best to respond to whatever arises in our lives.

When you have a regular meditation practice and you come back over and over and over again to how your body feels and to your breath and what's actually happening around you, over and over after you've been caught up in wondering what's going to happen tomorrow or making a grocery list or whatever you're doing, that creates a quiet, calm center over time.
And that quiet, calm center is something you can come back to when you want to.

Imagine being able to respond to impermanence and difficult situations from a calm, quiet center, from a grounded place, versus just saying or doing whatever the first thing is that comes up in your mind.
So I'm making a pitch for a regular meditation practice.
Impermanence isn't always a problem.
Sometimes a difficult stretch at work ends and things become more relaxed again, or after an accident or an illness, good health returns.
Sometimes an unexpected or unwanted job loss can later lead to a better job, or a difficult relationship ends, but later you get into a better one.
My mother lived to be almost 103 and she was pretty healthy and active until her mid to late 90s, but the last few years were really tough.

She was almost blind and almost deaf and she couldn't recognize faces and she couldn't hear what people were saying, so she couldn't socialize and she couldn't read and she couldn't watch television and she couldn't even listen to recordings.
So she suffered a lot and she handled it really well, but she very much wanted to die and she kept asking my sister, who was a doctor, can you bring me a pill, so I can get done with this.
And it was really painful for us to just watch her suffer.
There was nothing we could do, and I think she was quite relieved to die.
I know we were just relieved that her suffering was over.
I don't know for sure what happens when people die, but it seemed to me her suffering was over, and we were glad for that.
So I want to make sure and be clear that working with impermanence and accepting it does not mean being passive or unfeeling about the losses in our lives.
It does not mean being above or avoiding the pain.
It's normal and healthy to grieve our losses, and grief has a real healing function.
In the same article that I mentioned earlier with Norman Fischer, he said this about grief.
*The happiness that spiritual practice promises is not endless bliss, endless joy, and soaring transcendence.
Who would want that in a world in which there is so much injustice and so much tragedy and so much unhappiness, illness, and death?
To feel the scourge of impermanence and loss and to appreciate it at the same time profoundly as the beautiful essence of what it means to be at all.
This is the deep truth I hear reverberating in the Buddha's last words.
Everything vanishes, practice goes on.*
So I'm going to finish with one more quote, and this is from a talk by Marjoleen Janssen.
She's a Vipassana teacher and she quoted a Sri Lankan monk, but I could not understand her pronunciation of his name.
So I don't have his name, but I do have his quote, which I will read to you.
*He said everything in the world changes, but there is something innocent in these changes.
Impermanence is innocuous in itself.
We say it is innocuous because it means no harm to anyone.
It is simply the nature of the world.
It can do us harm only when we grasp.*
So that's what I have to say about impermanence, and thank you very much for your attention.
I usually give a kind of short Dharma talk, and so there's time, I think, for, if we want, breaking into little groups or just staying in one big group and having questions and stuff.
Either one is fine with me.
I have a couple of questions I could have little groups discuss if you want to do that.
Okay, I don't know, maybe we go into groups of three and each person will have two minutes to make a comment, and then I'll ring a bell and the next person and the next person.
And why don't you organize yourself in groups and then I'll tell you what things you could talk about if you want to.
I bet you guys can do your own little group.
I don't have to put you in a breakout room, right?
Because I don't know how to.
We'll see what happens.
Deborah and Eileen, can you hear me?
**Participant:** I can.
**Seishu John Wiley:** Oh, okay, I see two more people, but I don't know how to put people into—
**Participant:** Yeah, there's four people here and yeah, if we put them in a breakout room.
Can you give them a discussion?
**Seishu John Wiley:** Okay, what I thought you could talk about is each person can maybe give one or two examples of impermanence that you've run into in your life and how you handled it.
And you could use any example you want, and you could use handling it in a way that you think was done well or a way that you thought made things more difficult.
Does everybody hear that?
**Participant:** Yes.
**Participant:** Jelis, did you realize we never heard any bells in the audio?
It was off and on and off and on the whole time.
**Seishu John Wiley:** Sorry to hear that.

**Participant:** Looks like [unclear: "original Soundtree Musicians"] is on, so I think that's a, I think we need a separate microphone for us, like a 360 microphone, because we can almost never hear the service.
Yeah, and it's a different computer every time.
I think we'll need to, that's a long term.
It'll be better in the new Dharma Hall, for sure.
**Seishu John Wiley:** All right, I'm going to send you into breakout room.
Okay.
Thanks for doing that.
Well, let's see, no recording.
Thank you.
